Whether, from Sir R. E. Stubbs' decision, suspension or expulsion was to be inferred is not clear from the wording of the resolution sent to the Education Committee, but there are indications that his successor is inclined to the more lenient view, and that during the period in which the door of local schools has been closed to them, the schoolboy will be considered to have explained their offences. The wisdom of such a course is evident, having regard to the fact that the students have already suffered as a result of their action—the rude awakening of certain students who thought that it was free education they were to get in a neighbouring so-called educational institution has already received publicity—also taking into consideration the state of genuine fear into which many of them were worked as a result of very extensive propaganda amongst them Hongkong educational institutions are necessary, quite apart from their general educative value, as a means of combating the Bolsnevik propaganda which is being so extensively organised in China to day and it would be a mistake to admit defeat and

text: It into the schools. The Reds Coast that they have captured all the Normal Schools of the country, and in a recent article, the Rev. A. W. Lochhead, resident in Honan for the past twenty-one years, states there is much to indicate that their boast has some foundation in fact. In North Honan he had had bitter personal experience that the Normal School was the centre of the most violent and anti-foreign propaganda and he had heard that one hundred and twenty Middle School teachers in the provinces had been dismissed because they were not Red. In considering their future policy the Hongkong Government have to bear in mind, not only the future of the students immediately concerned, but also the dissemination of propaganda which by personal contact with others each student is capable of spreading. If the doors were permanently closed against these students in Hongkong infinite harm might be done and if the balance is truly to be struck between justice, generous consideration and expediency some such action as the Government are accredited with intending would appear to be the wishes course.

label: text

label: text
text: A "Government Gazette Extraordinary" issued yesterday announces.—

label: text
text:
"Whereas the day of the funeral of Her late Majesty Queen Alexandra is to be one of Public Mourning," His Excellency, the Governor in Council directs that Friday, November 27, 1935, shall be observed in this Colony as a dies non, under and with the effect mentioned in section 7 of Ordinance No. 5 of 1912.
A memorial service will be held in St. John's Cathedral at 10 o'clock to which all classes of the community are invited. A limited number of seats will be reserved for the Legislative Council, Consuls, Navy and Army Officers, Government Officials, heads of business houses and soldiers and sailors. The North Transept, Chapel, Baptistry and parts of the Navy and side circles will be open to the general public. The seating capacity of the Cathedral is 700 with additional standing room for about

label: text
text: capacity of the Cathedral is 700 with additional standing room for about 300.

label: text
text: The congregation is asked to be seated by 9:15 a.m. Music will be played at 9:50.

label: text
text: The service will last about 40 minutes. There will be no sermon.

label: text
text: At St. Andrew's Church, Kowloon, a memorial service will be held at 10 a.m. to tomorrow and the Rev. J. Horace Johnston, of Union Church, will take part.

label: text
text: A special memorial service will be held by the Parsee Community of Hongkong to-morrow at the Parsee Church when the head priest will hold a Jason ceermony and recite prayers and invocations in memory of the late Queen Mother. In these the Parsee Community will join.

text: Several motor accidents took place yesterday resulting in injuries to pedestrians.

text: At the foot of Garden Road, a Chinese coolie was knocked down by a motor car which was taking the turn from Queen's Road. The man's injuries necessitated his removal to the Government Civil Hospital.

label: text
text: A Chinese student who was driving a motor car along Nathan Road collided with a public ricsha near St. Andrew's Church. The vehicle was overturned and damaged to the extent of $40; the coolie also receiving severe bruises. An offer made by the student to settle the incident by a voluntary payment of $35 to the ricsha farmer and $10 to the injured coolie was declined, and the parties were taken to the Police Station.
